A specific temperature on the skin

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
I distract myself with something else

Threat.value: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I have lost my connection to my community and culture

vignette: Kofi's eyes scan the rearview mirror, his gaze darting between the faces of his passengers and the darkening streets outside. As a taxi driver, he's grown accustomed to the rhythms of the city, but certain sounds still make him tense: the crunch of gravel beneath tires, the creak of leather seats, or – worst of all – the soft thud of footsteps behind him. It's a sound that can transport him back to his childhood home, where his caregiver's approach would signal another bout of physical abuse. One particular memory stands out: being forced to stand under a scalding shower as punishment for some minor transgression. The sensation of burning skin has left an indelible mark on Kofi's psyche. Even now, when the air conditioning in his cab kicks in or a passenger adjusts the temperature, he can feel a fleeting sense of panic – as if his body is still primed to respond to that long-ago threat. As a result, Kofi has grown wary of intimacy. He keeps his relationships superficial, hesitant to let anyone get too close for fear of being hurt again. His friends and family have begun to notice the distance he maintains, but Kofi can't seem to shake the feeling that vulnerability is a luxury he can no longer afford. When emotions become overwhelming, Kofi reaches for distractions: his phone, video games, or – increasingly – marijuana. He's convinced himself that these coping mechanisms are harmless, even necessary, given the stress of his job and the lingering trauma from his past. Yet, as the months have passed, he's started to notice a disturbing pattern: his risk-taking behavior has escalated, whether it's speeding through intersections or accepting rides in sketchy neighborhoods. Despite his bravado, Kofi can't shake the sense that danger lurks around every corner. He finds himself constantly on high alert, scanning the surroundings for potential threats – even when there are none. His friends have commented on his "paranoia," but to Kofi, it's simply a necessary precaution in a world he no longer trusts. The cumulative effect of these behaviors has been isolating. Kofi feels disconnected from his community and culture, as if he's lost touch with the very things that once brought him comfort. He looks around at his friends, who seem carefree and whole, and wonders what happened to the boy he used to be – before the abuse, before the fear took hold. Recently, a close friend was hospitalized after a violent mugging, and Kofi's reaction was visceral: an overwhelming sense of dread, coupled with a certainty that he should have been there to protect his friend. In the aftermath, as he struggled to process his emotions, Kofi realized that he needed help – not just to manage his symptoms but to confront the underlying fears that had taken hold. As he sits in the therapist's office, Kofi feels a glimmer of hope. Perhaps, with time and support, he can learn to distinguish between real threats and the echoes of his past. Maybe, one day, he'll be able to trust others – and himself – enough to form genuine connections once more. For now, though, he takes a tentative step forward, acknowledging that the road to healing will be long, but determined to reclaim some semblance of control over his life.
